provenance.verification: See docs/differentiation-original-20261030.md for checks actually performed.

marking_policy: Maths4U indicative marking guidance, not an official examination-board mark scheme. Award stated criteria once each, up to the part maximum. Accept valid equivalent methods. Follow-through applies only where explicitly stated; do not award an accuracy criterion for an incorrect final result.

lessons.title: Derivatives: powers, linear inner functions and domains
lessons.objective: Find first and second derivatives and interpret a derivative as an instantaneous slope.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: use integer and fractional indices, expand brackets and simplify algebra.

The derivative is the limiting slope of a secant:

\[f^{\prime}(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}h.\]

In the quotient h≠0, and x+h must remain in the function's domain. A finite derivative gives the tangent gradient, not the ordinate f(x). Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity alone does not guarantee a derivative: |x| has a corner at zero.

The power rule is \(\frac d{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}\) wherever the real-valued power is differentiable. Constants differentiate to zero; add derivatives term by term and retain constant multipliers. Rewrite reciprocals as negative powers and roots as fractional powers first. Negative powers require x≠0. The fractional-power calculations in this block use positive bases to avoid ambiguous real branches and endpoint derivatives.

For a constant exponent and a linear inner function,

\[\frac d{dx}(ax+b)^n=na(ax+b)^{n-1}.\]

Include the inner derivative a. Check the original and derivative domains: a square root can exist at an endpoint where its derivative is not finite. Differentiate again to obtain f″, applying the rules afresh. Expand a polynomial product first when no product rule is needed.

Recall later

\(y=4x^3-7\) has y′=12x² and y″=24x. The constant contributes nothing to either derivative.

examples.solution_html: Term by term, \(y^{\prime}=15x^2+8x^{-3}\). The two minus signs in the negative-power term cancel. The original exclusion x≠0 remains.
Write \(y=x^{1/2}+6x^{-1}\). Thus \(y^{\prime}=\tfrac12x^{-1/2}-6x^{-2}=1/(2\sqrt{x})-6/x^2\), on the stated positive domain.

examples.question_html: Find the first and second derivatives of \(y=(2x-1)^5\).
examples.solution_html: \(y^{\prime}=5(2x-1)^4(2)=10(2x-1)^4\). Differentiating once more gives \(y^{\prime\prime}=10(4)(2)(2x-1)^3=80(2x-1)^3\). Both inner multipliers are needed.

common_mistakes: Reducing an exponent without multiplying by its original value.
Forgetting the derivative of the linear inner function.
Substituting an excluded value or assuming every root endpoint has a finite derivative.

lessons.title: Tangents, normals and the zero-gradient case
lessons.objective: Find tangent and normal equations at a point and handle a horizontal tangent correctly.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: differentiate a function and use point–slope line equations.

At a point \(P=(a,f(a))\) where f′(a) is finite, the tangent is

\[y-f(a)=f^{\prime}(a)(x-a).\]

Find both the point and the slope. A derivative value is not a line equation until it is paired with a point. For a finite nonzero tangent slope m, the normal has slope −1/m and passes through the same point.

If m=0, the tangent is horizontal, y=f(a), and the normal is vertical, x=a. Do not divide by zero or report a numerical infinite slope. The formula above assumes an ordinary finite derivative; a vertical tangent requires separate reasoning.

For a tangent parallel to a known line, equate f′(x) to that line's slope and solve for every permitted x. Substitute each x into the original function to obtain the points. A nonmonotonic derivative can give more than one point.

Recall later

A tangent of slope −3 has a normal of slope 1/3. A horizontal tangent has a vertical normal.

examples.question_html: Find the tangent and normal to y=x² at x=1.
examples.solution_html: The point is (1,1) and y′=2x gives m=2. The tangent is \(y-1=2(x-1)\), or y=2x−1. The normal is \(y-1=-\tfrac12(x-1)\), or y=−x/2+3/2.

examples.question_html: Find the tangent and normal to y=x²+3 at x=0.
examples.solution_html: The point is (0,3), with gradient zero. The tangent is y=3 and the normal is x=0. The latter is a vertical line, not y=0.

examples.question_html: Find every point on y=x³−x whose tangent is parallel to y=2x+5.
examples.solution_html: Set 3x²−1=2, obtaining x=±1. Both ordinates are zero, so the points are (−1,0) and (1,0). Their tangents are y=2x+2 and y=2x−2 respectively.

common_mistakes: Using f(a) as the slope instead of f′(a).
Using a reciprocal without changing its sign for a normal.
Losing a second parallel-tangent point or dividing by a zero tangent slope.

lessons.title: Increasing, decreasing and stationary points
lessons.objective: Use derivative signs, classify stationary points and compare candidates for an absolute extremum.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: factor derivatives, solve inequalities and read signs on intervals.

Where f′>0 throughout an interval, f is strictly increasing; where f′<0, it is strictly decreasing. At a differentiable stationary point f′=0. A zero derivative alone does not establish a maximum or minimum: inspect the behaviour around the point.

  • A change in f′ from positive to negative gives a local maximum.
  • A change from negative to positive gives a local minimum.
  • No sign change may give a stationary point that is neither; investigate the curve.

If f′(a)=0 and f″(a)>0, the second derivative test gives a local minimum; f″(a)<0 gives a local maximum. If f″(a)=0, the test is inconclusive. A stationary point of inflection has a horizontal tangent and a change of concavity. Derivative signs or the actual function can resolve an inconclusive test.

A strictly increasing function can have an isolated zero derivative, as x³ does at zero. Do not split a monotonic interval merely because a derivative touches zero without changing sign.

A local extremum concerns nearby inputs. An absolute extremum concerns the entire stated domain. On a closed bounded interval, compare all interior stationary points, any interior points where a derivative fails, and the endpoints of a continuous function. On an open or unbounded domain, an endpoint or limiting value may not be attained.

Recall later

f′(a)=f″(a)=0 means “test inconclusive”, not “definitely an inflection”. Further reasoning is essential.

examples.question_html: Find the stationary points and monotonic intervals of f(x)=x³−3x.
examples.solution_html: \(f^{\prime}=3(x-1)(x+1)\) is positive for x<−1 and x>1, negative for −1<x<1. The local maximum is (−1,2) and local minimum (1,−2), using the sign changes.

examples.question_html: Classify the stationary point of f(x)=x³.
examples.solution_html: f′=3x² vanishes only at zero and is positive on both sides. Thus zero is not a maximum or minimum. Since f″=6x changes from negative to positive, (0,0) is a stationary point of inflection. The function is strictly increasing on the real line.

examples.question_html: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x)=x²−4x+7 on 0≤x≤5.
examples.solution_html: f′=2x−4 gives the interior candidate x=2. Compare f(0)=7, f(2)=3 and f(5)=12. The absolute minimum is 3 at x=2; the absolute maximum is 12 at the included endpoint x=5.

common_mistakes: Assuming every stationary point is a turning point.
Treating f″=0 as a conclusive classification.
Ignoring endpoints or reporting a local extremum as an absolute one without comparison.

lessons.title: Related rates and small increments
lessons.objective: Relate changing quantities through a derivative, keeping signs, units and approximation status.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: differentiate powers, use geometric formulas and convert units consistently.

If y=f(x) and x changes smoothly with time t, the chain rule gives

\[\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{dy}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}.\]

Evaluate the geometric derivative at the specified instant. A negative rate means a quantity is decreasing; it is not an instruction to discard a solution. If a volume has units cm³ and time has units s, its rate has units cm³/s, while a radius rate has units cm/s.

For a small change Δx, the linear estimate is \(\Delta y\approx f^{\prime}(x)\Delta x\). Use the derivative at the initial x. The exact change is f(x+Δx)−f(x); the two need not agree. Similarly, over a short time step, \(x(t+\Delta t)\approx x(t)+\dot x(t)\Delta t\). This is a local approximation, not permission to assume the rate stays constant indefinitely.

Recall later

If y=x², then Δy=2xΔx+(Δx)² exactly. The first-order estimate omits (Δx)².

examples.question_html: A sphere has V=4πr³/3. At r=2 cm, dr/dt=0.1 cm/s. Find dV/dt.
examples.solution_html: \(dV/dr=4\pi r^2\), so \(dV/dt=4\pi(2^2)(0.1)=1.6\pi\) cm³/s. Both the sign and the volume-per-time units are retained.

examples.question_html: An area y=3x² cm² depends on a length x cm. At x=5, dx/dt=−0.4 cm/s. Find dy/dt.
examples.solution_html: \(dy/dx=6x\), so \(dy/dt=6(5)(-0.4)=-12\) cm²/s. The area is decreasing at 12 cm²/s.

examples.question_html: Use differentiation to estimate the change in x² when x increases from 4 to 4.03; compare with the exact change.
examples.solution_html: Δx=0.03 and f′(4)=8, so Δy≈8(0.03)=0.24. The exact change is 4.03²−4²=0.2409. The linear estimate is low by 0.0009, the omitted square (0.03)².

common_mistakes: Confusing a geometric derivative with a time derivative.
Dropping a negative rate or using inconsistent length/volume units.
Writing an approximate small-increment relation as an exact finite change.

lessons.title: Optimisation on a feasible domain
lessons.objective: Build a one-variable model, reject inadmissible stationary values and justify a global optimum.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: eliminate a variable from a constraint, differentiate, and interpret derivative signs.

  1. Define the variables and state a feasible domain from the geometry or context.
  2. Use the constraint to write the objective as a function of one variable.
  3. Find stationary candidates and retain only those inside the feasible domain.
  4. Classify candidates, compare appropriate boundary values or limits, and justify the optimum on the whole domain.
  5. Give the requested dimensions or quantity with units, retaining exact values before rounding.

A negative second derivative at a stationary point proves a local maximum; it does not by itself prove a global maximum on an arbitrary domain. A complete derivative-sign argument, a suitable comparison with endpoints/limits, or an algebraic bound can establish the global result.

Geometric dimensions are usually positive. A root that gives a negative side, a zero-volume object or a dimension beyond the sheet is not admissible. On an open domain, boundary limits help compare values without pretending the boundary objects are feasible.

Recall later

For A=x(12−x), \(A=36-(x-6)^2\le36\). Equality occurs at the feasible value x=6, so the bound proves the global maximum directly.

examples.question_html: A rectangle has perimeter 24 cm. Find its greatest area and dimensions.
examples.solution_html: If the sides are x and y, x+y=12, so A=x(12−x), with 0<x<12. A′=12−2x vanishes at x=6. It is positive before 6 and negative afterwards, giving the global maximum 36 cm² at a 6 cm by 6 cm square.

examples.question_html: Find the least value of f(x)=x+9/x for x>0.
examples.solution_html: \(f^{\prime}=1-9/x^2=(x-3)(x+3)/x^2\). The only positive stationary input is 3. The derivative is negative on (0,3) and positive on (3,∞), proving the global minimum f(3)=6. The negative root is outside the domain.

examples.question_html: An open-top cylinder has volume 8π cm³. Minimise the area of its base and curved surface.
examples.solution_html: With r>0, the height is h=8/r² and the area is \(A=\pi r^2+16\pi/r\). Its derivative is \(2\pi(r^3-8)/r^2\), negative for 0<r<2 and positive for r>2. Hence the global minimum occurs at r=2 cm, h=2 cm, with A=12π cm².

common_mistakes: Solving the stationary equation without stating or checking a feasible domain.
Using only a local second-derivative test to claim a global optimum.
Giving an optimal input but omitting the requested output, other dimension or units.

problems.title: A polynomial with a repeated stationary factor
problems.objective: Differentiate twice and find all points with horizontal tangents.
problems.hint_html: Differentiate term by term, then factor the first derivative before solving for horizontal tangents.

parts.prompt_html: Find f′(x) and express it as a product of factors.
parts.solution_html: Differentiate each nonconstant term: f′=12x³−24x²+12x. Taking out 12x leaves x²−2x+1=(x−1)², so \(f^{\prime}=12x(x-1)^2\).

criteria.requirement: Differentiate the quartic and cubic terms correctly.
Differentiate the quadratic and constant terms correctly.
Factor the complete derivative as 12x(x−1)².

parts.alternative_methods: Expand and then factor, or use an equivalent correct differentiation method.
parts.common_error: Differentiating the constant as a nonzero term or losing the repeated factor.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find f″(x).
parts.solution_html: Differentiate the expanded first derivative to get \(f^{\prime\prime}=36x^2-48x+12\).

criteria.requirement: Differentiate the cubic and quadratic terms of f′ correctly.
Give the complete second derivative 36x²−48x+12.

parts.alternative_methods: Differentiating an equivalent factored expression correctly is accepted.
parts.common_error: Reusing the original exponents instead of differentiating f′.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find every point on the curve where the tangent is horizontal.
parts.solution_html: Horizontal tangents require 12x(x−1)²=0, so x=0 or 1. Substituting into the original function gives f(0)=−5 and f(1)=3−8+6−5=−4. The points are (0,−5) and (1,−4). A repeated root is counted once.

criteria.requirement: Find both and only stationary inputs 0 and 1.
Obtain the corresponding ordinates −5 and −4.
Give the two points, with no duplicated root.

parts.alternative_methods: Solving the unfactored derivative and checking each point is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving only x-values or assuming the repeated root is not a stationary point.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A radical and a reciprocal
problems.objective: Use rational powers and a linear inner derivative on a stated positive domain.
problems.hint_html: Rewrite the radical and reciprocal as powers. Keep the factor 3 from the linear inner function at each differentiation.

parts.prompt_html: Find g′(x).
parts.solution_html: Write \(g=(3x+1)^{1/2}+2x^{-1}\). The radical contributes \(\tfrac12(3x+1)^{-1/2}(3)\), while the reciprocal contributes −2x⁻². Hence \(g^{\prime}=3/(2\sqrt{3x+1})-2/x^2\), valid for x>0.

criteria.requirement: Apply the outer half-power derivative correctly.
Include the inner multiplier 3.
Differentiate 2/x as −2/x² and give the complete result.

parts.alternative_methods: Any algebraically equivalent exact expression on the stated domain is accepted.
parts.common_error: Omitting the inner derivative or giving a positive derivative for 2/x.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find g″(x).
parts.solution_html: Differentiate \((3/2)(3x+1)^{-1/2}\): the coefficient becomes (3/2)(−1/2)(3)=−9/4 and the exponent is −3/2. The second term −2x⁻² differentiates to 4x⁻³. Thus \(g^{\prime\prime}=-9/[4(3x+1)^{3/2}]+4/x^3\).

criteria.requirement: Obtain the radical-part exponent −3/2.
Obtain its full coefficient −9/4, including the second inner multiplier.
Give the reciprocal-part derivative 4/x³ and the complete result.

parts.alternative_methods: Equivalent denominator or negative-index notation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Applying the inner derivative only during the first differentiation.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find g′(1) and interpret its sign for the curve near x=1.
parts.answer_html: \(g^{\prime}(1)=-5/4\); the curve is decreasing near x=1.
parts.solution_html: \(g^{\prime}(1)=3/(2\sqrt4)-2=3/4-2=-5/4\). The derivative is continuous and negative at this interior point of the positive domain, so it stays negative in a sufficiently small neighbourhood. The curve is decreasing there; this statement does not assert that it decreases for every positive x.

criteria.requirement: Evaluate the exact gradient −5/4.
Interpret it as a negative slope/decreasing behaviour near the stated input.

parts.alternative_methods: A correct local tangent-slope interpretation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Treating the negative gradient as a negative ordinate or claiming global decrease.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A normal meets the horizontal axis
problems.objective: Use one point and derivative to construct two perpendicular lines and an intercept.
problems.stem_html: The curve is \(y=x^3-2x+1\). The point P has x-coordinate 2.
problems.hint_html: Find the ordinate from the curve, not the derivative. Both lines must pass through P.

parts.prompt_html: Find the coordinates of P and the tangent gradient at P.
parts.solution_html: At x=2, y=8−4+1=5. Since dy/dx=3x²−2, the gradient is 12−2=10.

criteria.requirement: Give P=(2,5).
Differentiate and evaluate to give gradient 10.

parts.alternative_methods: A first-principles gradient calculation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the ordinate 5 as the tangent slope.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find equations of the tangent and the normal at P.
parts.solution_html: The tangent is y−5=10(x−2), hence y=10x−15. The normal slope is −1/10, so y−5=−(x−2)/10, giving y=−x/10+26/5.

criteria.requirement: Give the correct tangent line through P.
Use normal slope −1/10.
Give the correct normal line through P.

parts.alternative_methods: Correct unsimplified point–slope equations are accepted.
parts.common_error: Using +1/10 or failing to pass the normal through P.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: The normal meets the x-axis at Q. Find Q.
parts.solution_html: Set y=0 in the normal: 0=−x/10+26/5, so x=52. Thus Q=(52,0). The intercept may be far from P; it belongs to the normal line, not necessarily to the cubic.

criteria.requirement: Set y=0 in the normal equation and solve for x.

parts.alternative_methods: Using the point–slope normal directly is accepted.
parts.common_error: Setting x=0, which would find a y-intercept.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Parallel tangents and a vertical normal
problems.objective: Solve a slope condition and treat a zero-gradient normal separately.
problems.hint_html: For part (a), match slopes rather than line intercepts. For part (c), do not divide by a zero slope.

parts.prompt_html: Find the point whose tangent is parallel to y=4x−7.
parts.solution_html: The derivative is 2x−6. Parallelism requires 2x−6=4, so x=5. Substitution into the curve gives y=25−30+11=6, hence (5,6).

criteria.requirement: Set the derivative equal to the required slope 4.
Solve for x=5.
Give the point (5,6).

parts.alternative_methods: A correct first-principles slope expression is accepted.
parts.common_error: Solving for an intersection with the given line instead of matching tangent slopes.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the normal at the point from (a).
parts.solution_html: The normal slope is −1/4 and the point is (5,6). Thus y−6=−(x−5)/4, or y=−x/4+29/4.

criteria.requirement: Use normal slope −1/4.
Give the correct line through (5,6).

parts.alternative_methods: Any equivalent exact line equation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the given line intercept −7 for the normal.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: At the vertex (3,2), state the tangent and normal equations and explain the normal direction.
parts.answer_html: Tangent y=2; normal x=3, because the tangent is horizontal.
parts.solution_html: At x=3, the derivative 2x−6 is zero. The tangent is horizontal, y=2; the perpendicular normal is vertical, x=3. A finite slope formula −1/0 is not used.

criteria.requirement: Give the horizontal tangent y=2.
Give the vertical normal x=3 with a perpendicular-to-horizontal explanation.

parts.alternative_methods: A correctly labelled sketch with both equations is accepted.
parts.common_error: Writing y=3 for a vertical line or treating −1/0 as a real slope.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Local extrema need not be the only absolute extrema
problems.objective: Build a derivative sign chart and compare all endpoint and interior candidates.
problems.stem_html: For real x, let \(f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1\). Part (c) restricts the domain to 0≤x≤4.
problems.hint_html: First factor f′. For the closed interval, evaluate both endpoints as well as the stationary inputs.

parts.prompt_html: Find the stationary points.
parts.solution_html: \(f^{\prime}=3x^2-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3)\). The stationary inputs are 1 and 3. Their ordinates are f(1)=5 and f(3)=1, so the points are (1,5) and (3,1).

criteria.requirement: Obtain and factor the correct first derivative.
Find both stationary inputs 1 and 3.
Give the corresponding points (1,5) and (3,1).

parts.alternative_methods: Solving the derivative quadratic by the formula is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving derivative values as ordinates.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: State the intervals of increasing and decreasing behaviour and classify both stationary points.
parts.answer_html: Increasing for x<1 and x>3; decreasing for 1<x<3. Local maximum (1,5), local minimum (3,1).
parts.solution_html: The signs of 3(x−1)(x−3) are +,−,+ on the three intervals. Thus f increases, then decreases, then increases. The positive-to-negative change at 1 gives a local maximum; the negative-to-positive change at 3 gives a local minimum.

criteria.requirement: Give both intervals with positive derivative.
Give the negative-derivative interval.
Classify the two points correctly with derivative-sign or valid second-derivative reasoning.

parts.alternative_methods: Use f″(1)=−6 and f″(3)=6 for classification, together with correct monotonic intervals.
parts.common_error: Reversing the middle sign or calling the stationary points absolute extrema on the whole real line.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: On 0≤x≤4, find the absolute maximum and minimum values and every x at which each is attained.
parts.answer_html: Maximum 5 at x=1 and 4; minimum 1 at x=0 and 3.
parts.solution_html: The candidate values are f(0)=1, f(1)=5, f(3)=1 and f(4)=5. Continuity and the derivative sign pattern account for the whole closed interval. The maximum is 5 at both 1 and 4; the minimum is 1 at both 0 and 3.

criteria.requirement: Evaluate both included endpoints and compare with the stationary values.
Give maximum 5 with both x=1 and x=4.
Give minimum 1 with both x=0 and x=3.

parts.alternative_methods: A complete sign-chart and endpoint-value argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Omitting the endpoint that ties an interior extremum.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A flat point without a turning point
problems.objective: Resolve an inconclusive second-derivative value and solve a slope inequality.
problems.hint_html: A square in h′ can touch zero without changing sign. Use h″ on both sides to investigate concavity.

parts.prompt_html: Find h′(x) and h″(x).
parts.solution_html: The linear inner derivative is 1, so h′=3(x−2)² and h″=6(x−2).

criteria.requirement: Give the correct first derivative.
Give the correct second derivative.

parts.alternative_methods: Expanding the cubic first is accepted.
parts.common_error: Losing the shift x−2 during differentiation.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find and classify the stationary point, explaining why it is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum.
parts.solution_html: h′=0 only at x=2 and h(2)=4. The derivative is positive on both sides, so the function increases through the point and has no local extremum there. Also h″ is negative before 2 and positive afterwards, proving a change of concavity. Hence (2,4) is a stationary point of inflection. The value h″(2)=0 alone would not prove this.

criteria.requirement: Find the stationary point (2,4).
Use the unchanged positive derivative sign or equivalent value comparisons to exclude a local extremum.
Show the concavity change and classify a stationary point of inflection.

parts.alternative_methods: The shifted-cubic form together with a correct monotonicity and concavity explanation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Calling every point with h′=h″=0 a point of inflection without further reasoning.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all x for which the tangent gradient is at least 12.
parts.solution_html: 3(x−2)²≥12 gives (x−2)²≥4, so x−2≤−2 or x−2≥2. Thus x≤0 or x≥4, including the equality endpoints.

criteria.requirement: Reduce to (x−2)²≥4 and select the outside branches.
Give x≤0 or x≥4 with both endpoints included.

parts.alternative_methods: A correct graph or absolute-value inequality argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Selecting the interval between the roots or excluding equality.
parts.label: c

problems.title: An expanding sphere has two different rates
problems.objective: Distinguish radius, volume and surface-area time derivatives.
problems.stem_html: A sphere has volume \(V=4\pi r^3/3\) and surface area \(A=4\pi r^2\). At a particular instant its radius is 4 cm and increases at 0.3 cm/s.
problems.hint_html: Differentiate each quantity with respect to r, then multiply by dr/dt at the stated instant.

parts.prompt_html: Find dV/dr in terms of r.
parts.solution_html: The constants remain as multipliers: \(dV/dr=(4\pi/3)(3r^2)=4\pi r^2\). This is a geometric derivative, not yet a time rate.

criteria.requirement: Apply the cubic power rule with the constant factor.
Give 4πr².

parts.alternative_methods: A correct difference-quotient derivation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using 4πr² directly as dV/dt without the radius rate.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find dV/dt at that instant, including units.
parts.solution_html: \(dV/dt=(dV/dr)(dr/dt)=4\pi(4^2)(0.3)=19.2\pi=96\pi/5\) cm³/s. The positive sign agrees with expansion.

criteria.requirement: Use the chain rule linking volume rate and radius rate.
Evaluate 96π/5 or an equivalent exact value.
Give volume-per-time units cm³/s and the positive rate.

parts.alternative_methods: A correctly evaluated decimal multiple of π is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving cm/s or omitting the factor 0.3.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find dA/dt at the same instant.
parts.solution_html: \(dA/dr=8\pi r\), so \(dA/dt=8\pi(4)(0.3)=9.6\pi=48\pi/5\) cm²/s. It is a different quantity with different units from the volume rate.

criteria.requirement: Use dA/dt=8πr dr/dt.
Give 48π/5 cm²/s or its equivalent.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent exact evaluation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Reusing the volume derivative or volume units for surface area.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A shrinking radius and a short-time estimate
problems.objective: Recover a signed length rate from a volume rate and use a stated local linearisation.
problems.stem_html: A cylinder has fixed height 12 cm and radius r cm, so \(V=12\pi r^2\) cm³. It changes smoothly. At a particular instant r=3 cm and \(dV/dt=-24\pi\) cm³/s. Use linearisation at that instant for the short-time estimate in (c).
problems.hint_html: Differentiate V with respect to time through r. A decrease in radius must keep its negative sign.

parts.prompt_html: Find dr/dt at the stated instant.
parts.solution_html: \(dV/dt=24\pi r\,dr/dt\). Thus −24π=24π(3)dr/dt, giving dr/dt=−1/3 cm/s.

criteria.requirement: Form dV/dt=24πr dr/dt.
Substitute the instantaneous radius and solve correctly.
Give −1/3 cm/s with the decreasing sign.

parts.alternative_methods: Using dr/dV as the reciprocal of the nonzero dV/dr is accepted.
parts.common_error: Dividing by r² or discarding the negative sign.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the rate of change of the diameter.
parts.solution_html: The diameter is D=2r, so dD/dt=2dr/dt=−2/3 cm/s.

criteria.requirement: Relate the diameter rate to twice the radius rate.
Give −2/3 cm/s.

parts.alternative_methods: Differentiating D=2r directly with respect to t is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the same numerical rate for diameter and radius.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Use a first-order estimate for the radius 0.06 s later.
parts.solution_html: \(\Delta r\approx(-1/3)(0.06)=-0.02\) cm, so r≈3−0.02=2.98 cm. This uses the initial instantaneous rate as a local linear approximation; it does not assert an exact constant radius rate over time.

criteria.requirement: Use Δr≈(dr/dt)Δt with the initial rate and Δt=0.06.
Give the approximate updated radius 2.98 cm.

parts.alternative_methods: A correctly stated linear model through the initial radius is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving 0.02 as the new radius or claiming the finite update is exact.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Three fenced sides beside a wall
problems.objective: Eliminate a constraint variable and prove a global area bound on the feasible domain.
problems.stem_html: A rectangular enclosure lies against a straight wall. Only the two sides perpendicular to the wall and the side parallel to it require fencing. There are 32 m of fencing, all used. Let each perpendicular side have length x m and the fenced parallel side have length y m; both lengths must be positive.
problems.hint_html: The constraint counts x twice. State the domain before searching for the greatest area.

parts.prompt_html: Express y and the area A in terms of x, and state the feasible domain.
parts.solution_html: The fence constraint is 2x+y=32, giving y=32−2x. Hence A=xy=x(32−2x)=32x−2x². Both x>0 and y>0 require 0<x<16.

criteria.requirement: Obtain y=32−2x from the three fenced sides.
Give A=32x−2x².
State the complete strict domain 0<x<16.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent expression using y as the independent variable is accepted if translated to the requested x form.
parts.common_error: Using the four-side perimeter or allowing a zero side.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Use differentiation to find the dimensions and area at the stationary candidate.
parts.answer_html: x=8 m, y=16 m; area 128 m².
parts.solution_html: A′=32−4x=0 gives x=8. Then y=32−16=16 and A=8(16)=128 m². The candidate satisfies the strict domain.

criteria.requirement: Differentiate and solve to obtain the feasible x=8.
Obtain the other dimension y=16 m.
Give the candidate area 128 m².

parts.alternative_methods: Any valid differentiation of an equivalent one-variable objective is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving only the optimal x and omitting the other dimension or area.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Justify that this is the greatest area over every feasible rectangle.
parts.solution_html: Completing the square gives A=128−2(x−8)²≤128 for every real x, with equality at x=8 in the feasible interval. This proves a global maximum. Alternatively A′ is positive for 0<x<8 and negative for 8<x<16, so the whole feasible domain rises then falls.

criteria.requirement: Give a valid global bound, or a complete derivative-sign/boundary argument on the feasible domain.
Show the bound is attained at the feasible candidate and conclude greatest area 128 m².

parts.alternative_methods: A negative second derivative together with a valid whole-domain concavity or endpoint-limit argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Asserting global optimality merely because A′ is zero.
parts.label: c

problems.title: An admissible cut from a rectangular sheet
problems.objective: Find the feasible stationary root of a cubic volume and verify a global maximum.
problems.stem_html: An open box is made from a 24 cm by 18 cm rectangular sheet. Equal squares of side x cm are removed from all four corners and the sides are folded upwards. The resulting box must have strictly positive height, length and width.
problems.hint_html: The cut x must be less than half the shorter sheet side. Keep both derivative roots until you have checked this constraint.

parts.prompt_html: Write the volume V as a polynomial in x and state its feasible domain.
parts.solution_html: The box dimensions are x, 24−2x and 18−2x. Thus V=x(24−2x)(18−2x)=432x−84x²+4x³. Strict positivity gives x>0, x<12 and x<9, hence 0<x<9.

criteria.requirement: Use all three correct dimensions in the volume model.
Expand to 432x−84x²+4x³.
State the complete feasible domain 0<x<9.

parts.alternative_methods: The factored volume is accepted alongside a correct polynomial expansion and domain.
parts.common_error: Using x<12 alone and overlooking the shorter side.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the feasible stationary value of x exactly, explaining any rejection.
parts.solution_html: V′=432−168x+12x²=12(x²−14x+36). Solving gives x=(14±√52)/2=7±√13. The plus value is about 10.606>9 and is infeasible; 7−√13≈3.39445 lies in (0,9).

criteria.requirement: Differentiate and obtain the correct stationary quadratic.
Find both exact roots 7±√13.
Retain only 7−√13 using the feasible domain.

parts.alternative_methods: Completing the square in the derivative equation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Keeping an algebraic stationary root that produces a negative box width.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the greatest volume, giving an exact expression and a value to 3 significant figures, and justify global optimality.
parts.solution_html: Let α=7−√13 and β=7+√13. V′=12(x−α)(x−β). On the feasible interval β>9, so V′>0 for 0<x<α and V′<0 for α<x<9. Thus α gives the global maximum; the boundary volume limits are zero. Substitution gives \(V(\alpha)=(7-\sqrt{13})(10+2\sqrt{13})(4+2\sqrt{13})=280+104\sqrt{13}\) cm³. This is approximately 654.977 cm³, or 655 cm³ to 3 significant figures.

criteria.requirement: Justify the global maximum over 0<x<9 by derivative signs or a complete candidate/boundary comparison.
Evaluate the exact greatest volume 280+104√13 cm³.
Give 655 cm³ to 3 significant figures.

parts.alternative_methods: A valid local classification plus complete comparison with boundary limits is accepted for global optimality; equivalent exact volume forms are accepted.
parts.common_error: Using only V″<0 to claim a global result without domain reasoning, or rounding x too early.
parts.label: c
